hints: Notice which curve is a straight line through the origin: for an ohmic metallic conductor at constant temperature $I$ is proportional to $V$.
Compare the two curved shapes: one has almost zero current $I$ at low $V$ then rises steeply, while the other starts steep then flattens as resistance increases with heating.
Recall that a semiconductor diode needs a threshold voltage before conducting, whereas a filament lamp heats up so its resistance rises and the $I$-$V$ gradient decreases.
walkthrough: Look at curve Y on the $I$ against $V$ axes. It is a straight line through the origin, so $I$ is proportional to $V$ and resistance $R = V/I$ is constant.
That constant-resistance behaviour is the metallic conductor at constant temperature, so Y is the ohmic conductor.
Look at curve X. The current $I$ is almost zero for small $V$ and then increases very rapidly after a threshold voltage.
That turn-on shape with negligible reverse or low-voltage conduction is characteristic of a semiconductor diode, so X is the diode.
Look at curve Z. It conducts immediately from the origin but the curve bends over, so the gradient $dI/dV$ decreases as $V$ increases.
Decreasing gradient means increasing resistance, caused by heating of the filament as current increases, so Z is the filament lamp.
Matching metallic conductor Y, diode X and filament lamp Z is option B. This is option B.

A.explanation: X is not ohmic because it is curved, and Z is not a diode because it conducts from $V = 0$.

B.explanation: Y is a straight line through the origin for an ohmic conductor, X stays near zero then rises sharply for a diode, and Z curves over for a filament lamp.

C.explanation: Z cannot be a diode because a diode has almost zero $I$ until a threshold $V$, whereas Z has large $I$ at small $V$.

D.explanation: Z is not ohmic because its $I$-$V$ graph is curved, and Y is not a diode because it conducts proportionally from the origin.
